newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti better off since return of Aristide - Preval.
newsitem.headline: Haiti better off since return of Aristide - Preval.

text.p: Two years after thousands of U.S. troops restored democratic government in Haiti, the Caribbean nation is better off despite persistent poverty and crime, Haitian officials said on Tuesday.

"Now we have a government chosen by the people," Haitian President Rene Preval said in a speech marking the second anniversary of the return from exile of former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide on Oct. 15, 1994.
Preval told Reuters that Haiti was a better place now, joking that he agreed with a statement made by Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole in an election debate.
Dole criticised President Bill Clinton's foreign policy record, saying he believed Rene Preval and Saddam Hussein were better off than they were four years ago.
"Of course I am better off," said Preval, laughing. "Four years ago I was living in exile."
The Haitian presidential palace was gleaming white and draped in flags to mark the anniversary.

The government, wanting to show it is cleaning house, used the occasion to issue new arrest warrants against leaders of the 1991 coup that overthrew Aristide and installed a bloody, three-year dictatorship.

The warrants were issued by the official prosecutor against former army chief of staff Phillipe Biamby and Yannick Cedras, the wife of coup leader Gen. Raoul Cedras, who are currently living in exile in Panama.
"They are wanted for various acts of corruption, for stealing property of the state," said Justice Minister Max Antoine.

Foreign Affairs Minister Fritz Longchamp said his advisors were deliberating over whether the government would file an extradition request to return Mrs. Cedras and Biamby to Haitian courts to answer charges against them.
The new warrants continued a high-profile fight against corruption that Preval launched last month after angry demonstrators demanded an improved justice system on the fifth anniversary of the coup.
Preval recently grilled an official of the government-run cement company and allegedly corrupt judges, who were taken away from the palace in handcuffs.
Preval joked on Tuesday that if he could find Cedras' wife, he would arrest her, too.
But Haitians said they were still furious that crimes seemed to go unpunished in their country and that the coup leaders were living in comfortable exile.
Haiti has severe unemployment, very high illiteracy and the Western Hemisphere's lowest standard of living.
"There were violent acts carried out against the people during the coup, and we want justice," said an old man who looked through the palace gates as officials sipped wine on the balconies.
Some 5,000 people are thought to have been killed during the three years of terrorific dictatorship, with tens of thousands more raped, tortured, beaten or forced into hiding.
